div.p: Utilization bound is a well-known concept first introduced in the seminal paper of Liu & Luyland which provides a simple and practical way to test the schedulability of a real-time task set. The original utilization boundfor the fixed-priority scheduler was given as a function of the num- ber of tasks in the periodic task set. In this papel; we define the utilization bound as a function of the information about the task set. By making use of more than just the number of tasks, we obtain various improvements over the Liu & Luyland bound. In particulal; we shall give a more intuitive derivation of the bound as a function of the number of harmonic chains in the task periods which allows us to derive a simpler algorithm to calculate such bounds. We derive algorithms that yield better bounds as a function of the period parameters of the task set. We also give a generalization of the bound for tasks whose deadlines are smaller than their periods.
'There are several technical loopholes in the proof of this bound in [IO], but the result is correct. A correct proof can be found in [4].

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Despite the tremendous amount of work and advances in real-time scheduling theory, the best results for schedulability testing of periodic task sets under the preemptive fixed priority scheduling policy provide only pseudo-polynomial under grant number N00014-99-1-0402. time algorithms. For periodic tasks whose deadlines are before their periods, the feasibility problem is co-NP-hard [9] if the initial requests can arrive at different points in time. In practice, pseudo-polynomial-time algorithms are often acceptable as compile-time (off-line) schedulability tests, as has been popularized in RMA (Rate Monotonic Analysis) [6]. As real-time applications grow in complexity, task sets become more dynamic in that their parameters may change at run time. For these applications, the pseudopolynomial-time schedulability tests may no longer be fast enough for use as admission tests in real time. In contrast, the concept of utilization bound provides a fast sufficiency test for schedulability. The classical Liu & Layland paper [lo] proves that, for a set of n periodic tasks whose deadlines are the same as their periods, the utilization bound under the preemptive fixed-priority scheduling policy and the rate monotonic priority assignment is n(2* -l).' Several other improvements and extensions on the utilization bound have been reported since then [7, 8, 11, 121. We shall show that the utilization bound of a task set can be more precisely determined if more information about the task set is exploited. The Liu & Layland bound n(2* -1) depends only on the number of tasks n in the task set [lo].

It can be improved to K ( 2 k -1) if the number of harmonic chains K in the task set periods is known [7] where K 5 n. We shall give a more intuitive derivation of this bound which allows us to derive a simpler algorithm for determining the number of harmonic chains for a given task set. If we make use of the period parameters in the task set, even better bounds can be derived as we shall show in the next section. Of course, if we make use of the execution times of the tasks as well, we can tell exactly if the task set is schedulable or not by performing a pseudopolynomial-time test, e.g., the critical-instant test as formulated in [2, 3, 51. As we have mentioned, this may not be practical as an on-line admission test for dynamic real-time systems. By revisiting the Liu & Layland proof, we shall derive algorithms which yield better bounds as a function of the period parameters of the task set, We also derive a generalization of the bound for tasks whose deadlines are smaller than their periods. Even though we consider only periodic tasks which start requesting at time 0, the results in this paper can be easily extended to sporadic tasks which have arbitrary request times and minimum separation times. In addition, we shall assume rate/deadline-monotonic assignment of priority and the use of the critical-instant test as a feasibility test throughout this paper.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 derives some bound improvements for the Liu & Layland model in which the deadline of a task is the same as its period. We call such tasks ( E , P)-type task sets. Section 3 considers ( E , D, P)-type task sets, i.e., tasks whose deadlines are different from their periods. Section 4 is the conclusion. We end this section by recalling some known results which we shall refer to in the rest of this paper.

An ( E , P)-type task set is a set of periodic tasks S = {Tl,T2 ,..., T,}, where Ti = (Ei,Pi), 1 5 i 5 n , and Ei, Pi are positive numbers denoting respectively the execution time and period of the task Ti. The utilization factor U of a set S of n tasks is C:=,2. Without loss of generality, we shall assume PI < P2 < ... < P,. By the rate monotonic assignment, 2' 1 has the highest priority and T, has the lowest priority. In this section, we shall derive better utilization bounds with the periods of the task k_nown. The task periods will be represented by the vector P = [PI, ..., P,]. Let us first take a look at an example.

Example 1 Consider a set of 6 tasks with periods forming a vector P' = [2,3,5,6,7,35]. The utilization bound of all sfch task sets is 0.7348 according to Theorem I . However; P can be formed from 4 harmonic chains. The harmonic chain bound according to Theorem 2 is 0.7568. Through exhaustive checking, we find that the exact utilization bound is 0.7952, Note that the exact bound is larger than both bounds calculated in Example l . The question is whether we can find an algorithm to calculate a better utilization bound, or even better, the exact bound. This section tries to answer this question. We shall start by defining two important concepts in Subsection 2.1 which are crucial for establishing our results. Subsection 2.2 defines the exact utilization bound and analyzes its properties. We give the formula of the exact utilization bound for a particular class of task sets in Subsection 2.3. In this paper, we shall not derive the exact bound for the general case but give instead some better bound algorithms in Subsection 2.4.

div.head: Exact Utilization Bound
div.p: Consider the class M of all ( E , P)-type task sets that cannot be scheduled by the preemptive fixed-priority scheduler. Let VEP be the greatest lower bound of the utilization factors of all such task sets in M . Any task set that has a utilization factor smaller than u~p is by definition schedulable by the RMA assignment of task priority. This is the basis of the utilization-bound based schedulability test. We call VEP the exact utilization bound and state its property formally below:

In [IO], it is claimed that "For a given fixed priority algorithm, the least upper bound of the utilization factor is the minimum of the utilization factor over all sets of tasks that fully utilize the processor" where a set of task fully utilizes the processor if increasing the execution time of any one of the task will result in unschedulability. This claim is true only if the minimum utilization factor of all fully utilizing task sets is the same as that of all critical task sets, since the class of fully utilizing task sets is properly contained in the class of critical task sets. Their derivation of the utilization bound turns out to require only extreme task sets and does not invalidate their result because the critical task sets in their proof happens to also extremely utilize the processor (please refer to [4]).

For the purpose of this paper, however, we need to take into consideration the distinction between extreme task sets and critical task sets. Specifically, if we focus on only those task sets characterized by a given task period array, the critical task set with the smallest utilization in this class of task sets may or may not extremely utilize the processor. In that case, if we only consider the extreme task sets, the bound we get may not be valid. We shall see to this situation later.

At this point, we should emphasize that the definition of the exact utilization bound depends on the class of task sets under discussion. In the derivation of the Liu & Layland bound, the authors considered all task sets of size n and derive a function of n which is the exact utilization bound.
